title: Science of Improvement
path: Quality Improvement in Healthcare and Patient Safety

headings.title: Introduction to the Science of Improvement in Healthcare
headings.content: The science of improvement is a structured, applied discipline that uses specific methods to drive measurable changes in health system performance, patient safety, and clinical outcomes. Unlike traditional research that asks what works under controlled conditions, improvement science asks how to make things work reliably within complex, everyday care environments. In resource-constrained settings like many Nigerian public hospitals, this discipline provides a framework to maximize existing resources rather than waiting for massive infrastructure overhauls. Every healthcare system is perfectly designed to get the results it currently gets; altering those outcomes requires intentional, scientific redesign of clinical processes.

headings.title: The Model for Improvement: Aim, Measures, and Changes
headings.content:
Developed by Associates in Process Improvement, the Model for Improvement provides a simple yet powerful framework for accelerating quality work. It rests on three fundamental questions that must be addressed before any testing begins:

1. **What are we trying to accomplish?**: This establishes the specific **aim statement**, detailing the magnitude of change and the target population within a defined timeframe.
2. **How will we know that a change is an improvement?**: This defines quantitative **measures**—outcome, process, and balancing measures—to track whether the interventions are actually working.
3. **What change can we make that will result in improvement?**: This identifies potential **change ideas** or interventions derived from evidence, clinical experience, or creative thinking.

headings.title: Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) Cycles in Nursing Practice
headings.content:
The **Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA)** cycle is the shorthand for testing a change in the real clinical world. It is iterative, meaning rapid, small-scale tests build upon one another until a change is ready for broader implementation.

- **Plan**: State the objective, formulate a prediction about what will happen, and outline the steps for the test, including who, what, where, and when.
- **Do**: Carry out the test on a very small scale—such as with a single patient, one shift, or a single nursing station—and document unexpected observations.
- **Study**: Analyze the data collected during the test, compare the results against the original predictions, and summarize what was learned.
- **Act**: Decide whether to adopt, adapt, or abandon the change idea before planning the next cycle.

headings.title: Process Mapping and Understanding Variation
headings.content:
Clinical processes are frequently more complex than they appear on the surface. **Process mapping**, or flowcharting, provides a visual representation of every step involved in delivering care, helping multidisciplinary teams identify bottlenecks, redundancies, and unnecessary delays. 

Once a process is understood, teams must examine **variation**. Not all variation is equal:
- **Common cause variation**: Natural, predictable fluctuations inherent in a stable process.
- **Special cause variation**: Unpredictable, sporadic spikes or drops caused by distinct, assignable events.

Run charts—graphs of data plotted over time—help clinical teams distinguish between these two types of variation, preventing reactive overcorrections to normal daily fluctuations.

headings.title: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Patient Safety
headings.content:
Errors in healthcare are rarely the result of careless individuals; rather, they stem from faulty systems that fail to support human performance. **Human factors engineering** studies how physical, cognitive, and organizational characteristics affect human interaction with equipment and environments. When designing safer systems, reliance on memory or vigilance is minimized. Instead, forcing functions, standardization, and checklists are implemented.

**Systems thinking** shifts the institutional culture away from blaming nurses or doctors toward analyzing why the system allowed an error to reach the patient. By viewing the hospital as an interconnected network of people, technology, and procedures, improvements can be engineered to make the right thing to do the easiest thing to do.

headings.title: Sustaining Improvements and Fostering a Culture of Quality
headings.content: Initiating a successful change is only half the battle; the greater challenge in healthcare is sustaining those gains over time. Initial enthusiasm often fades, causing clinical units to revert to old habits once formal project oversight ends. To prevent regression, successful changes must be embedded into standard operating procedures, orientation programs, and daily shift handovers. Leadership commitment, transparent feedback loops, and psychological safety—where staff can report errors and suggest improvements without fear of retribution—are essential for nurturing a lasting institutional culture dedicated to continuous quality improvement.
